title: Tool Results & Error Handling
summary: A tool call rarely returns a clean answer on the first try — APIs time out, inputs are wrong, records are missing. The job of tool result handling is to return structured, model-readable results (success or failure) and to surface errors back to the model as observations so it can retry, adjust arguments, or give up gracefully. The one rule that never bends: a tool exception must never crash the agent loop.

subtopics.title: Return structured results, not bare strings
subtopics.explanation: A tool should return a consistent, typed shape — usually a dict or object with a status field, data, and an optional error — so both your code and the model can tell success from failure without guessing. A raw string like 'not found' is ambiguous: is it data or an error? Giving every tool the same result envelope is what lets the loop handle any tool's outcome uniformly.

subtopics.title: Surface errors to the model as observations
subtopics.explanation: When a tool fails, the natural instinct is to raise — but the model can't see a Python traceback. Instead you feed the error text back as the tool's observation so the model reads it on the next turn and can react: fix a bad argument, try a different tool, or ask the user. Turning an error into an observation is what makes an agent able to recover instead of dying.

subtopics.title: Retry transient failures, give up on permanent ones
subtopics.explanation: Not all failures are equal: a network blip or 503 is transient and worth retrying (ideally with backoff), while a 404 or validation error is permanent and retrying just wastes calls. You classify the error, retry the transient kind a bounded number of times, and immediately surface the permanent kind to the model. Distinguishing the two is the difference between resilient tools and an agent that hammers a dead endpoint.

subtopics.title: Bound every tool with a timeout
subtopics.explanation: A tool that hangs forever silently freezes the whole agent, so each call needs a hard time limit after which you abort and return a timeout error. You wrap the call in a timeout mechanism (a signal, a thread with a deadline, or an async wait_for) and convert the expiry into a normal failed result. A timeout is just another surfaced error — it keeps a slow dependency from stalling the loop.

subtopics.title: The loop must survive any tool exception
subtopics.explanation: The dispatcher that runs tools is the last line of defense: it wraps every execution in try/except so that no matter what a tool throws — a bug, a bad argument, an unexpected None — the loop catches it, records a failed observation, and continues. If one tool crash can kill the run, the agent is not production-ready. A crash-proof dispatcher is what turns a fragile demo into an agent that degrades gracefully.

foundations.overview: In an agent, a tool call is a fragile boundary between the model's plan and the messy real world: the network fails, arguments are wrong, records don't exist, and dependencies hang. Robust tool handling has four parts. First, every tool returns a structured result — a consistent envelope with a success flag, data, and an optional error — so outcomes are unambiguous. Second, failures are surfaced to the model as observations (readable error text), not raised as exceptions the model can't see, so it can retry, fix arguments, or fall back. Third, you classify failures: transient ones (timeouts, 503s) get bounded retries with backoff, while permanent ones (404s, validation errors) are reported immediately instead of retried. Fourth, every call is time-bounded so a hung dependency can't freeze the loop. Underpinning all of it is one non-negotiable rule: the dispatcher wraps execution in try/except so a tool exception is turned into a failed observation and the loop keeps running. Together these turn tools from a crash risk into a recoverable, self-healing part of the agent.
foundations.formalDefinition: Tool result handling is the discipline of executing a model-requested tool inside a protective boundary that (1) returns a structured result envelope for both success and failure, (2) converts exceptions and timeouts into observations the model reads on its next turn, (3) retries transient errors under a bound while failing fast on permanent ones, and (4) guarantees the agent loop never terminates due to a tool raising.
foundations.whyItMatters: Autonomous agents run unattended and call unreliable dependencies dozens of times per task; if any single failure crashes the loop or is hidden from the model, the agent either dies or blunders on with corrupt state. Structured, surfaced, bounded error handling is what lets an agent recover on its own and is the practical line between a demo and a system you can trust in production.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each tool as an intern making a phone call for you. If the line is busy (transient), they redial a couple of times; if the number is disconnected (permanent), they stop and tell you. They never just hang on hold forever (timeout), and if they trip over the cord (exception), they don't take the whole office down — they write 'call failed: line disconnected' on a note and hand it back so you can decide what to do next.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Coding agents reporting a failed test or compile error back to the model, research agents retrying a rate-limited search API, support agents handling a 'no order found' lookup by asking the user for a correct id, and data agents timing out a runaway warehouse query instead of hanging the session.
foundations.performanceImpact: Bounded retries with exponential backoff smooth over transient blips without hammering a struggling dependency, and per-call timeouts cap the worst-case latency of the whole loop; misclassifying permanent errors as retryable, by contrast, multiplies cost and latency for no benefit.
commonUseCases: Returning a uniform success/error envelope from every tool
Feeding API and validation errors back to the model for recovery
Retrying transient failures with backoff, failing fast on permanent ones
Timing out slow tools so a hung call can't freeze the loop

commonMisconceptions.myth: If a tool fails, the agent should raise and stop.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Raising crashes the loop and hides the error from the model. Catch it, return a failed result, and surface the error text so the model can react and recover.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should always retry a failed tool call.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only transient failures (timeouts, 503s) deserve retries. Retrying a 404 or a validation error just wastes calls and money — classify first, then retry the transient kind only.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A timeout is a special exceptional case.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A timeout is just another failed result. You convert the expiry into the same error envelope so the model handles it exactly like any other tool failure.

interactiveExamples.title: A crash-proof dispatcher with a result envelope
interactiveExamples.explanation: Every tool call goes through one dispatcher that returns a uniform {ok, data, error} envelope and never lets an exception escape. A good tool, a missing tool, and a throwing tool all produce a result the loop can handle the same way.

code.caption: Three very different outcomes, one shape. The loop never sees a raised exception, so a bad tool can't crash the run.

interactiveExamples.title: Classify, retry transient, surface the error to the model
interactiveExamples.explanation: A flaky tool fails twice with a transient timeout, then succeeds; a second tool hits a permanent 404 and is not retried. On final failure the error becomes an observation the model would read next turn.

code.caption: The timeout is retried until it succeeds on attempt 3; the 404 is permanent, so it fails immediately after one call.
code.expectedOutput:
{'ok': True, 'data': 'weather: 18C', 'error': None} after 3 attempts
{'ok': False, 'data': None, 'error': '404 order not found'}

codeLab.title: Build a resilient tool runner
codeLab.instructions: Implement run_tool(tools: dict, name: str, args: dict) -> dict that safely executes a model-requested tool and always returns an envelope {"ok": bool, "data": any, "error": str | None}. It must (1) return {"ok": False, ...} with a helpful error if the tool name is not in tools, (2) call the tool with **args and return {"ok": True, "data": <return value>, "error": None} on success, and (3) catch ANY exception the tool raises and return {"ok": False, "data": None, "error": "<ExceptionType>: <message>"} without ever propagating the exception. Complete the function so the harness passes.

    # {"ok", "data", "error"} envelope. NEVER let an exception escape.
    ...

codeLab.testHarness:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def explode():
    raise RuntimeError("kaboom")

tools = {"add": add, "explode": explode}

ok = run_tool(tools, "add", {"a": 2, "b": 3})
assert ok == {"ok": True, "data": 5, "error": None}, ok

missing = run_tool(tools, "nope", {})
assert missing["ok"] is False and "nope" in missing["error"], missing

boom = run_tool(tools, "explode", {})
assert boom["ok"] is False and "RuntimeError" in boom["error"], boom

# bad arguments must also be caught, not raised
bad = run_tool(tools, "add", {"a": 1})
assert bad["ok"] is False, bad
print("all tests passed")
hints: Use tools.get(name) so a missing tool gives None instead of raising a KeyError.
Wrap the fn(**args) call in try/except Exception so bad arguments (TypeError) and any runtime error are both captured.
Format the error as f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}" so the model gets both the error class and the message.

checkpoints.prompt: A tool call raises an exception mid-loop. What should the dispatcher do?
options: Re-raise so the whole agent stops
Catch it, return a failed result, and feed the error text back as an observation
Silently swallow it and return an empty string
checkpoints.explanation: The model can't see a Python traceback. Catch the exception, return a structured failed result, and surface the error as an observation so the model can retry, fix arguments, or give up — the loop keeps running.

checkpoints.prompt: Which failure is worth retrying (rather than failing fast)?
options: A validation error on a required field
A request timeout / 503 from a busy service
checkpoints.explanation: Timeouts and 503s are transient — the same call may succeed shortly after, so a bounded retry with backoff is appropriate. 404s, validation errors, and unknown-tool errors are permanent; retrying them just wastes calls.

checkpoints.prompt: This runner is supposed to keep the loop alive on tool failure. Why doesn't it?
options: tools[name] raises KeyError for unknown tools, and only ValueError is caught — any other exception (TypeError, RuntimeError, TimeoutError) still escapes and crashes the loop
You cannot return a dict from a tool
checkpoints.explanation: Two holes let exceptions escape: tools[name] raises KeyError for an unknown tool, and catching only ValueError lets every other exception (bad args -> TypeError, timeouts, etc.) propagate. Use tools.get(name) and except Exception.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the timeout guard so a hung tool becomes a failed result instead of freezing the loop.

import concurrent.futures as cf
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as ex:
    future = ex.submit(fn)

checkpoints.explanation: future.result(timeout=5) waits at most 5 seconds and raises cf.TimeoutError if the tool hasn't returned, which you catch and convert into a failed result — so a hung dependency can't stall the agent loop.

theory.question: Why should a failed tool call surface the error to the model instead of raising an exception?
theory.directAnswer: Because the model can't see a Python traceback — it only sees the conversation. If you raise, the loop crashes and the model never learns what went wrong. If you catch the failure and feed the error text back as the tool's observation, the model can read it next turn and recover: fix a bad argument, try a different tool, or ask the user.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A pattern where every tool exception or failure is converted into a structured, model-readable observation (an error string in the tool result) rather than propagated as an exception.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Agents run unattended and depend on unreliable systems; a raised exception both crashes the loop and hides the cause from the only component that could react to it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The dispatcher wraps tool execution in try/except, builds a {ok: False, error: ...} envelope, and appends it to the message history as a tool/observation message, so the next model call reasons over the failure just like any other result.

theory.whyImportant: It's the mechanism that lets an agent self-heal — recovering from failures on its own is the core difference between a fragile demo and a production agent.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent calls get_order('A-999'), which doesn't exist; instead of crashing, the tool returns 'no order found', the model reads it and asks the user to confirm the order number.

followUps.question: Should the error text be raw or sanitized?
followUps.answer: Sanitize it: give the model a concise, actionable message without secrets, internal stack traces, or PII, since the error goes into the prompt and possibly to the user.

followUps.question: What if the same tool keeps failing?
followUps.answer: Bound the retries and, on exhaustion, surface a terminal 'this tool is unavailable' so the model stops calling it rather than looping forever.

theory.question: How do you decide whether to retry a failed tool call or give up?
theory.directAnswer: Classify the failure. Transient errors — timeouts, connection resets, 503/429 rate limits — may succeed if tried again, so retry them a bounded number of times with exponential backoff. Permanent errors — 404 not found, 400/validation errors, unknown tool, auth failures — will not fix themselves, so fail fast and surface them to the model immediately.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An error-classification-and-retry policy that distinguishes recoverable transient failures from deterministic permanent ones.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Blindly retrying everything wastes calls, money, and latency on errors that can never succeed, while never retrying makes the agent brittle to normal network flakiness.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inspect the exception type or status code, map it to transient vs permanent, retry the transient set up to a cap with backoff (and optional jitter), and on permanent errors or exhausted retries return a failed observation the model can act on.

theory.whyImportant: Correct classification directly controls both resilience and cost — it's what keeps an agent robust to blips without hammering a dead endpoint.
theory.realWorldExample: A research agent's search API returns 429; the runner backs off and retries, succeeding on the second attempt, while a 404 from a document lookup is reported to the model at once so it picks a different source.

followUps.question: Why add backoff and jitter?
followUps.answer: Backoff gives a struggling service time to recover, and jitter prevents many agents from retrying in lockstep and creating a thundering herd.

followUps.question: Where should the retry live — in the tool or the loop?
followUps.answer: Usually inside the tool/runner layer so the model isn't burdened with low-level retries; the loop only sees the final success or a surfaced failure.

scenario.question: Your agent occasionally hangs for minutes and, separately, sometimes dies with an unhandled exception when a tool throws. How would you make the loop robust?
scenario.directAnswer: Add a crash-proof dispatcher that wraps every tool call in try/except and returns a structured failed result, and put a hard per-call timeout on each tool so a hung dependency aborts into a timeout error. Classify errors so transient ones retry with backoff and permanent ones fail fast, and surface all failures to the model as observations. Cap total retries so the loop can't spin forever.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A resilience overhaul that adds a protective boundary (dispatcher + timeout + retry policy) around tool execution.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The hangs come from unbounded tool calls with no timeout; the crashes come from exceptions escaping the dispatcher — both violate the rule that a tool problem must degrade into a surfaced observation, not a stall or a crash.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Wrap execution in try/except Exception returning {ok: False, error}, run each call under a timeout (thread/async deadline), classify caught errors as transient vs permanent, retry the transient set under a bound with backoff, and append every outcome to history so the model reacts.

scenario.whyImportant: It converts the two most common production agent failure modes — silent hangs and hard crashes — into bounded, observable, recoverable events.
scenario.realWorldExample: After wrapping a slow warehouse-query tool in a 10s timeout and the dispatcher in try/except, a runaway query now returns 'timed out after 10s' and the agent retries a narrower query instead of freezing the session.

followUps.question: How do you keep the timeout from leaking threads?
followUps.answer: Use cancellation-aware primitives (async wait_for, or a worker with a real cancel path); a plain thread that ignores the timeout keeps running, so prefer cooperative or process-level cancellation for truly blocking calls.

followUps.question: What global guardrail complements per-call handling?
followUps.answer: A max-steps and total-time/cost budget on the whole loop, so even repeated recoverable failures can't run up unbounded cost.

coding.question: Write a retry wrapper that retries only transient errors up to a bound with exponential backoff, returns a structured result, and never raises.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want one function that runs a callable, classifies each exception as transient or permanent, retries only the transient kind up to a cap, and always returns an {ok, data, error} envelope. I inject the sleep function so the test runs instantly, and I use a set of transient markers to keep classification simple and explicit.
lineByLine: TRANSIENT lists substrings that mark a retryable failure; is_transient checks the error message against them.
call_with_retry loops attempt 0..retries, so retries=3 means up to 4 total tries.
On success it returns immediately with {ok: True, data, error: None}.
On exception it returns a failed envelope if the error is permanent OR the last attempt is used up — it never re-raises.
Otherwise it sleeps 2**attempt seconds (injectable, so tests pass a no-op) and retries.
The __main__ block shows a flaky tool succeeding on attempt 3 and a permanent 404 failing after a single call.
coding.timeComplexity: O(retries) tool invocations in the worst case; backoff time dominates wall-clock but not step count.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only the last result envelope is held.

followUps.question: How would you add jitter?
followUps.answer: Sleep a random fraction of the backoff window (e.g. random.uniform(0, 2**attempt)) so concurrent agents don't retry in lockstep.

followUps.question: Why inject sleep instead of calling time.sleep directly?
followUps.answer: It makes the retry logic deterministic and instant to unit-test, and lets you swap in async sleep in an async runner.

keyTakeaways: Give every tool one structured result envelope ({ok, data, error}) so success and failure are unambiguous for both your code and the model.
Surface failures to the model as observations instead of raising — that's what lets the agent retry, fix arguments, or gracefully give up.
Classify errors: retry transient ones (timeouts, 503/429) with bounded backoff, but fail fast on permanent ones (404, validation, auth).
Put a hard timeout on every tool call so a hung dependency becomes a normal failed result instead of freezing the loop.
The dispatcher wraps every tool in try/except — a single tool exception must never crash the agent loop.
